content: Endometrial hyperplasia is a condition characterized by an excessive proliferation of the endometrial cells, which form the inner lining of the uterus. This condition is associated with an increased gland-to-stroma ratio within the endometrial tissue. The majority of cases of endometrial hyperplasia are caused by elevated levels of estrogen that are not adequately counteracted by progesterone or progesterone-like hormones. These hormones typically mitigate the proliferative effects of estrogen on the endometrium. Anovulation, or the absence of ovulation, can lead to prolonged estrogen exposure and a relative deficiency of progesterone, resulting in excessive stimulation of the endometrial tissue. Estrogen stimulation in this context may originate from either endogenous (internal) or exogenous (external) sources. Endometrial hyperplasia can be classified histologically into two main types: simple and complex. Additionally, it can be categorized based on the presence or absence of cellular atypia, resulting in two subtypes: hyperplasia with cellular atypia and hyperplasia without cellular atypia. It is essential to differentiate endometrial hyperplasia from other conditions that may present with similar ultrasound findings. These include normal endometrial thickening during the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle, sessile endometrial polyps, submucosal uterine fibroids, endometrial cancer, adherent intrauterine blood clots, and pregnancy. Endometrial hyperplasia can occur in women of all age groups, but it is more commonly observed in postmenopausal women. Most cases, except for complex atypical hyperplasia, tend to resolve spontaneously over time. However, if left untreated, approximately 30% of patients with atypical hyperplasia may progress to develop endometrial carcinoma. Malignant transformation into endometrial cancer is the most common complication of endometrial hyperplasia. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally favorable. Pelvic ultrasound performed between days 5 and 10 of the menstrual cycle can help reduce variability in endometrial thickness measurements and may aid in the diagnosis of endometrial hyperplasia. On ultrasound, the condition is typically characterized by a homogeneous increase in endometrial thickness. However, asymmetric or focal thickening with surface irregularity may also occur, which should raise suspicion for malignancy. Progesterone therapy is the preferred medical treatment for benign endometrial hyperplasia. The management approach depends on the patient’s desire for future childbearing. For atypical endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, total hysterectomy is considered curative. A positive history of irregular menstrual cycles, such as in polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD), may be present in patients with endometrial hyperplasia. A detailed drug history, including inappropriate hormone replacement therapy in postmenopausal women or tamoxifen use in breast cancer patients, may also provide valuable insights into potential risk factors. Physical examination findings in patients with endometrial hyperplasia are usually unremarkable, and routine laboratory tests are typically normal. However, some patients may exhibit abnormal complete blood counts suggestive of anemia due to prolonged vaginal bleeding. There are no specific findings associated with endometrial hyperplasia on CT or MRI imaging. Pelvic ultrasound remains the primary imaging modality for diagnosis. Hysteroscopy may also be useful for direct visualization of precancerous lesions. Definitive diagnosis is typically achieved through curettage of the uterine cavity to obtain endometrial tissue for histopathological analysis. Common risk factors for developing endometrial hyperplasia include age over 35 years, white race, nulliparity, late menopause, early menarche, tamoxifen therapy, obesity, Lynch syndrome, a history of diabetes, gallbladder disease, thyroid disease, and a family history of ovarian, colon, or uterine cancers. Routine screening for endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma is not recommended.
